title: Crypto ally Tom Emmer elected House GOP minority whip
summary: The Minnesota lawmaker, who helped establish the Congressional Crypto Caucus, will stay on as Republican whip after Democrats won the midterms.
content:
Pro-crypto US Representative Tom Emmer has been elected House Republican minority whip, securing the party’s second-highest leadership position as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January.

Emmer beat Texas Representative August Pfluger in a 103-76 secret ballot vote, according to Politico. He previously served as House Republican majority whip and will remain the party’s No. 2 leader, this time under incoming Minority Leader Jim Jordan.

As minority whip, Emmer will be responsible for rallying Republican votes, coordinating the party’s legislative strategy and helping maintain unity on key bills.

Emmer has been a leading Republican voice on digital assets. In March 2025, he and Representative Ritchie Torres announced the bipartisan Congressional Crypto Caucus, aimed at mobilizing support for digital asset legislation, including stablecoin and market structure bills.

He is also an original cosponsor of the CLARITY Act and introduced the Blockchain Regulatory Certainty Act, which seeks to clarify that blockchain developers and infrastructure providers who do not control customer funds are not money transmitters under federal law.

“Tom has been one of the strongest advocates for digital assets in Congress, and he has led the fight against a government-controlled CBDC and stood up for American innovators,” GOP Senator Cynthia Lummis said on X.

Related: US midterm elections 2026 as it happened: Democrats win control of Congress

title: Coinbase, Kalshi and Other Firms Back CFTC in Fight Over Stock Perpetuals
summary: Six firms filed a proposed friend-of-the-court brief backing the CFTC's authority in the single-stock perpetual futures case. A judge earlier denied…
content:
A dispute over who may regulate perpetual futures linked to individual US stocks is drawing some of crypto’s most prominent companies into federal court. Coinbase, Kalshi, Kraken parent Payward, DRW, Jump Trading and Paradigm have sought permission to support the Commodity Futures Trading Commission in litigation brought by the Capital Markets Alliance Association. Their proposed intervention follows approvals for new stock-linked perpetual products earlier this month.

TL;DR: Six firms filed a proposed friend-of-the-court brief backing the CFTC’s authority in the single-stock perpetual futures case. A judge earlier denied emergency relief but questioned the regulator’s legal basis for the approvals. The court has not delivered a final ruling on whether the products should remain available.

Why the legal issue is more complicated than crypto versus Wall Street

A perpetual futures contract provides economic exposure to price changes without a preset expiration date. It is a familiar structure in cryptocurrency markets. Applying the design to an individual listed US company raises a separate statutory question: which agency’s rules govern the product, and what obligations attach to the exchange listing it?

The Capital Markets Alliance argues that these contracts belong within the securities-law framework rather than under the CFTC’s treatment of security futures. The companies supporting the regulator argue that the law permits the agency’s approach and that blocking the products would limit US-listed alternatives to offshore markets. Those are legal positions advanced in an active dispute, not findings that either side has finally won.

The stakes extend beyond where an order is matched. Classification influences customer protections, margin rules, market surveillance and whether a new product can lawfully be offered to eligible participants.

The judge’s November 3 order matters

In the published federal court order, Judge Valerie Caproni denied a request for a temporary restraining order. That means the plaintiff did not obtain an immediate halt at that stage. The reasoning, however, was not a broad endorsement of the CFTC’s authority. The judge indicated the plaintiff was likely to succeed on the statutory question but had not demonstrated the imminent irreparable harm required for emergency relief.

That distinction is essential. A failed emergency application is not the same as a judgment that the products comply with the law. A preliminary-injunction dispute and the broader merits can still produce further decisions, and both sides may submit additional arguments.

Tokenized shares and stock perps are not equivalent

NewsBTC recently examined the NYSE’s proposed tokenized securities venue. That project is about representing and settling security ownership. A stock perpetual gives a trader a derivative claim whose value is linked to a share; it does not necessarily transfer ownership of that share or its voting and dividend rights.

Likewise, our coverage of Ripple Prime’s round-the-clock RWA-linked swaps illustrates how conventional markets can be referenced by crypto-native derivatives. The legal treatment of each product depends on its structure and jurisdiction, not simply the fact that it can trade 24 hours a day.

What happens now

The immediate questions are whether the judge accepts the proposed outside briefs, how the plaintiff’s latest reply addresses the statutory objections, and what relief the court considers appropriate. There is no basis to describe the matter as settled or to assume that every stock perp listing has permanent authorization.

The case is a serious test of how US financial regulation adapts to perpetual trading conventions. Its outcome could influence the shape of future listings, but the facts today support a narrower statement: the CFTC’s approvals are being challenged, and the industry is organizing a legal defense.

Written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.

title: US Targets $456K in Crypto Allegedly Tied to Dating Site, Facebook Fraud
summary: Federal prosecutors sought forfeiture of cryptocurrency allegedly taken through romance fraud targeting people on dating sites and Facebook. The Massachusetts case followed failed withdrawals from fake investment platforms and efforts to trace payments made by victims. Prosecutors Pursue Funds Trace...
content:
Federal prosecutors sought forfeiture of cryptocurrency allegedly taken through romance fraud targeting people on dating sites and Facebook. The Massachusetts case followed failed withdrawals from fake investment platforms and efforts to trace payments made by victims.

Key Takeaways

  • Prosecutors targeted 456,602 USDT, valued at $456,602.
  • Investigators traced alleged proceeds to two wallets and seized funds.
  • Ownership claims must be resolved before assets can return to victims.

Prosecutors Pursue Funds Traced to Romance Fraud

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Massachusetts said Nov. 9 that it had filed a civil forfeiture action targeting 456,602 USDT, valued at approximately $456,602. Its romance fraud forfeiture action involved alleged schemes targeting people in Massachusetts and elsewhere. Authorities had traced the proceeds to two cryptocurrency wallets and seized the funds.

According to the complaint, perpetrators cultivated trust through online dating sites and Facebook before encouraging cryptocurrency investments on fake platforms. The office stated:

“Although victims believed they were sending funds to a legitimate cryptocurrency investment platform and earning profits, in reality those funds were sent to unhosted cryptocurrency wallets (wallets not hosted on a cryptocurrency exchange).”

Victims realized they had been scammed when withdrawal attempts failed, even after they paid purported fees and taxes.

Fraudulent Platforms Encourage Larger Deposits

The FBI describes cryptocurrency investment fraud as a process that can begin with a romance or confidence scam before shifting to investment pitches. Fraudulent platforms may display fictitious gains or permit early withdrawals to encourage larger deposits. Subsequent demands for taxes or fees provide another means of extracting money from victims.

Impersonation also features in fake cryptocurrency exchanges and unsolicited investment offers. Fraudulent services may copy legitimate websites, while unsolicited contacts promise investment returns. These approaches rely on an appearance of credibility to persuade people to transfer assets.

Separate federal investigations have targeted larger sums through similar forfeiture proceedings. Five complaints announced in July sought more than $25 million in seized cryptocurrency. The largest involved approximately $12.1 million connected to romance scams affecting more than 200 victims; another targeted about $10.4 million linked to fraudulent investment platforms.

Ownership Claims Precede Returns to Victims

Massachusetts prosecutors also pursued a separate crypto ATM fraud forfeiture action announced July 31. That case sought approximately $47,000 allegedly taken through technology-support and government-impersonation schemes. Investigators identified five victims whose payments reached the same wallet.

Cross-border recovery efforts have likewise required further steps after seizure. Ghanaian and British authorities seized $15.1 million linked to an investment scam, as described in June. The assets were liquidated into an exhibit account managed by Ghanaian authorities. Authorities were screening victims ahead of planned restitution, or repayment for losses.

In the Nov. 9 case, the complaint’s claims remained allegations. Civil forfeiture allows third-parties, meaning others asserting ownership of the assets, to present claims that must be resolved before forfeiture and any return to victims.

title: Walt Launches Standalone Crypto App After Years Inside Telegram
summary: Walt has launched a separate Android app while keeping its existing Telegram integration. The service advertises access to more than 200…
content:
The wallet platform that grew up inside Telegram is trying to become a destination in its own right. Walt, previously branded Wallet in Telegram, launched a standalone Android app on November 10. The company says an iOS version will follow. For the first time, customers can sign up without using Telegram, with Google and Apple among the supported account routes.

TL;DR: Walt has launched a separate Android app while keeping its existing Telegram integration. The service advertises access to more than 200 cryptocurrencies, tokenized US stocks and ETFs, perpetual futures and yield products, subject to regional availability. iOS is planned, not already live as part of today’s announcement.

The real change is distribution

The new app largely bundles products Walt had already developed inside Telegram. That means the headline is not the invention of a new trading contract or token. The commercial difference is that Walt no longer needs a user to start in a messaging app before becoming a customer.

According to the company’s product announcement, the app offers more than 200 cryptocurrencies, over 100 tokenized US stocks and exchange-traded funds, and perpetual contracts linked to crypto and some traditional asset classes. Walt also advertises yield features and AI-assisted research and trading tools. Availability and restrictions differ by jurisdiction and by individual product.

The company’s rebranding guidance explains that Walt and Telegram’s separate Money wallet are different services. That matters for users who remember an older ‘Wallet’ label and could easily assume the products now share an operator or custody arrangement.

One account across two interfaces

Walt says existing users can sign in through Telegram and access the same funds through the standalone app. New users can register without Telegram. This shared-account design may reduce the inconvenience of switching channels, but users should still confirm the account recovery, security and withdrawal rules of the actual wallet service they use.

There is also an important distinction between owning a tokenized representation of a US stock and holding the original share through a conventional brokerage account. Product terms determine shareholder rights, corporate actions and redemption. NewsBTC’s coverage of transfer agents in tokenized securities describes why those legal and operational details are central to a credible market.

NewsBTC has also examined Visa’s institutional stablecoin settlement expansion. That infrastructure serves a different audience, but it underlines how wallet apps and payment networks are both trying to make digital balances more usable outside speculative trading.

The new app’s perpetual futures are another product that deserves clear risk labeling. They provide leveraged or derivative exposure rather than ownership of the underlying asset, and can carry liquidation and funding risks even when presented in a convenient mobile interface.

Can a messaging wallet win a place on the home screen?

Walt’s distribution advantage has been access to Telegram users, but downloads, funded accounts and repeated use are different measures. The company says it has a large registered audience without publishing a full current breakdown of active users and trade volumes in this announcement. Those are the numbers that would help measure the standalone app’s impact.

The next milestones are an iOS release, geographic availability, fees and the adoption of products users cannot obtain as conveniently in the Telegram interface. Walt has now delivered the separate app. Whether customers will make it their primary home for digital assets remains an open commercial question.

Written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.

title: Binance Blocks MEXC Transfers After $16B Illicit Finance Allegations
summary: Binance restricted dealings with MEXC after U.S. authorities alleged the exchange facilitated at least $16 billion in illicit transactions. The move followed a designation targeting MEXC’s access to the U.S. financial system. Binance Rejects MEXC Transfers and Withholds Deposits Binance said Nov. 10...
content:
Binance restricted dealings with MEXC after U.S. authorities alleged the exchange facilitated at least $16 billion in illicit transactions. The move followed a designation targeting MEXC’s access to the U.S. financial system.

Key Takeaways

  • Transfers from Binance to MEXC-linked addresses will be rejected.
  • Incoming deposits face compliance reviews and possible account closures.
  • FinCEN’s order takes effect 30 days after Federal Register publication.

Binance Rejects MEXC Transfers and Withholds Deposits

Binance said Nov. 10 that it was restricting transactions involving MEXC following the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network’s (FinCEN) designation of the exchange as a primary money laundering concern. Its immediate transaction restrictions covered MEXC, MEXC Global, affiliates, and related entities. The exchange advised users against sending, receiving, or otherwise transacting through Binance involving those businesses.

The company stated:

“Requests to send funds to MEXC addresses will be rejected.”

Under its MEXC deposit restrictions, incoming funds from the listed businesses would be temporarily withheld for compliance review. Account holders could face further limitations, including removal from the platform.

Among the covered entities were MEXC Global Limited, MEXC Singapore Pte Ltd, and GIDA Technology AG. FinCEN identified GIDA as a Swiss entity among MEXC’s current or former affiliates. Binance’s list also included other corporate entities, trading names, and affiliates across multiple jurisdictions.

FinCEN Alleges $16 Billion in Illicit Transactions

The U.S. Treasury Department disclosed the action against MEXC Global on Nov. 6 as part of Operation Economic Outcast, a U.S. campaign to disrupt the Iranian government’s financial networks. Officials alleged that the exchange facilitated at least $16 billion in illicit transactions between May 2021 and May 2026. Treasury linked the activity to Iranian, North Korean, and Russian sanctions evasion, as well as cybercrime.

Those alleged illicit flows included nearly $1.5 billion connected to Russian sanctions evasion, according to Treasury. That figure included $232 million in direct transactions with entities sanctioned by the United States, the European Union, and the United Kingdom. Officials also cited dealings with Russia-based sanctioned exchange Garantex and its successor, crypto exchange Grinex.

FinCEN issued its order under the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act, which authorizes Treasury to restrict transactions involving foreign financial institutions linked to Russian illicit finance. The measure prohibits U.S. financial institutions from transmitting funds to or from MEXC Global. It takes effect 30 days after publication in the Federal Register.

Customers Report Frozen Funds as Exchanges Tighten Controls

Some MEXC users reported frozen deposits at OKX after transferring what they described as their own assets between exchanges. Founder and CEO Star Xu said OKX had strengthened its controls before the regulatory deadline and treated FinCEN special measures with caution similar to sanctions. He warned that associated funds could be frozen and accounts investigated.

MEXC CEO Vugar Usi noted that the company had begun an independent review of its anti-money laundering and sanctions controls. He added that it intended to engage constructively with FinCEN. In its response to FinCEN’s order on Nov. 7, MEXC said it was operating normally, and user assets remained secure.

In February, Binance had outlined its broader compliance monitoring program, stating that it proactively removed high-risk accounts. The company reported processing more than 71,000 law enforcement requests globally in 2025. It also described investments of hundreds of millions of dollars in transaction monitoring and counter-terrorist financing infrastructure.

Beyond direct transfers into trading accounts, Binance’s notice covered indirect dealings involving the listed businesses. Such activity could breach its terms of use and trigger temporary restrictions on impacted funds and accounts during review. The company directed affected users to contact Binance Support through official channels.

title: LNbits rushes emergency patch after reported Bitcoin wallet thefts
summary: The project warned that installations running older versions were vulnerable and urged operators to replace potentially exposed credentials even after upgrading.
content:
Bitcoin Lightning wallet platform LNbits has urged users to update immediately to its latest version after reporting a wave of attacks targeting LNbits instances that resulted in stolen funds. 

The project published version 1.7.0 on Tuesday, describing it as a critical release addressing vulnerabilities and strengthening authentication, extension management and payment handling. LNbits warned that updating alone would not protect installations whose credentials had already been compromised.

“It’s been a very challenging few days, working relentlessly to get the v1.7 release out after our users and we suffered losses,” LNbits creator Ben Arc said on X. 

LNbits provides software for running Bitcoin Lightning wallets and payment applications, including merchant checkouts, tipping services and paywalls. Developer Ben Arc said in May that about 200,000 people run the software themselves.

LNbits first warned operators on Sunday to disable its Paywall extension while it investigated a potential vulnerability. Just over an hour later, the project urged users to shut down their LNbits servers immediately, citing a wave of attacks. It also took its own hosted installations offline. 

The company has not yet detailed the exploit and how many were impacted by it. In an announcement accompanying the emergency patch, LNbits said the vulnerability affects all versions before 1.7.0 and puts funds at risk of theft.

Related: BitMart founder says security team ‘severely understaffed’ after new hack

It also warned that credentials exposed before upgrading could still give attackers access afterward, urging operators to reset wallet keys, replace funding-source credentials and treat secrets stored in LNbits settings as compromised and recommended moving to a fresh server if a compromise is suspected.

Cointelegraph reached out to Ben Arc and LNbits for comment.

One user, Kevin Ravensberg, said attackers exploited his LNbits instance, withdrawing about 2.3 million satoshis, or 0.023 Bitcoin, through newly created accounts before he could shut down the server.

The company said a separate report detailing the exploit would follow.

title: Charles Schwab Opens Live Solana, Avalanche and Chainlink Trading to Eligible Clients
summary: Schwab Crypto now supports SOL, AVAX and LINK trading for eligible retail clients, adding to its BTC and ETH offering. Schwab says its service became…
content:
Charles Schwab has moved three major altcoins from its expansion plan into its live crypto trading menu. The brokerage announced on November 9 that eligible Schwab Crypto clients can now trade Solana, Avalanche and Chainlink, alongside Bitcoin and Ethereum. The distinction between ‘planned’ and ‘available’ is the new milestone here.

TL;DR: Schwab Crypto now supports SOL, AVAX and LINK trading for eligible retail clients, adding to its BTC and ETH offering. Schwab says its service became broadly available to qualifying customers in October 2026. The announcement concerns direct crypto trading, not approval of new exchange-traded funds for these tokens.

Why the launch timing matters

Schwab began offering early access to its crypto service in May and opened it to eligible retail clients in October. The November addition broadens a product already running in the market, rather than announcing a future concept with no users. That gives the three altcoins a route to customers who prefer established brokerage infrastructure and account management over a separate crypto-native trading platform.

NewsBTC covered the earlier Schwab expansion plan in August. The new press release supplies the operational update those readers would have been waiting for: the named assets are available, subject to Schwab’s account and jurisdiction requirements.

This is an important qualification because access is not universal. Customers must qualify for the service, and conventional brokerage protections or product terms should never be assumed to apply identically to every digital-asset holding. Investors should read the published risk disclosures and custody arrangement rather than relying on the familiarity of the corporate brand.

Three assets, three different exposures

Solana is a smart-contract network whose economic activity includes trading, payments and tokenized assets. Avalanche operates a different blockchain ecosystem with an emphasis on customizable network infrastructure. Chainlink is associated with data and connectivity services used by smart contracts. They are all crypto assets, but they are not interchangeable bets on a single technology.

That distinction helps explain why broadening a brokerage menu does not immediately establish institutional conviction in any particular network. A broker chooses instruments for a combination of liquidity, client interest, operational readiness and risk controls. Adding a symbol is a meaningful access decision; it is not a research conclusion that the asset must outperform.

For further ecosystem context, NewsBTC’s recent look at Solana’s network upgrades and tokenized-asset activity shows why a network’s technical evolution should be assessed separately from the price of a token on a brokerage screen.

Adoption is a different question from availability

The launch raises useful questions: how many customers will open or fund Schwab Crypto accounts, how much activity will flow into the new assets, and whether more tokens follow? The announcement does not provide day-one trading volumes or say how much demand each token will receive.

A larger, more familiar distribution channel could change the market over time by widening who can participate. But whether it deepens liquidity or simply moves existing traders from one provider to another will require actual usage data. For now, the verified news is an operational launch with a clearly defined set of supported coins.

Written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.

title: Dormant Bitcoin Data Reveals 227,196 BTC in Pre-2019 Coins Revived in 2026
summary: Bitcoin’s sleeping giants have been stirring this year, and the numbers are staggering. Checkonchain data reveals that more than 227,000 BTC acquired before 2019 have awakened in 2026, while a separate onchain investigation into dormant wallets uncovers a trail of colossal transfers, mysterious whal...
content:
Bitcoin’s sleeping giants have been stirring this year, and the numbers are staggering. Checkonchain data reveals that more than 227,000 BTC acquired before 2019 have awakened in 2026, while a separate onchain investigation into dormant wallets uncovers a trail of colossal transfers, mysterious whale movements, and ancient mining rewards dating back to 2010.

Key Takeaways

  • Ancient bitcoin wallets are awakening in 2026, with some coins stirring after more than 16 years of silence.
  • Mysterious, precisely timed transfers suggest certain sleeping whales may be following a carefully coordinated pattern.
  • Two blockchain datasets reveal a far bigger story about dormant bitcoin, and the oldest holders aren’t necessarily the busiest.

Bitcoin.com News examined two distinct datasets to investigate the revival of long-dormant bitcoin holdings throughout 2026. The first is a tool called Btcparser 1, which monitors inactive bitcoin addresses and records their outgoing transactions, providing a detailed account of individual wallet movements, transaction sizes, and historical activity.

The second, the Bitcoin network analytics provider Checkonchain, tracks revived bitcoin supply according to when coins were acquired, offering a broader perspective on how much older supply has returned to circulation. Together, these sources reveal when dormant bitcoin moved, which generations of holders were most active, and how the activity compares with the larger pool of revived coins.

Btcparser Data Shows Nearly 34,000 BTC Moved From Sleeping Bitcoin Wallets in 2026

According to Bitcoin.com News’ examination of Btcparser’s onchain records, dormant addresses established between 2010 and 2017 transferred approximately 33,932.19 BTC, worth $2.49 billion today, across 873 recorded movements between January and October 2026. That translates into an average of roughly 112 BTC daily, although activity varied considerably from one month to another.

The movements unfolded in distinct waves, featuring enormous single-day transactions, coordinated wallet sweeps, and occasional appearances by coins that had remained untouched for more than 16 years. Some addresses transferred their entire balances within seconds of one another, while others displayed patterns suggesting carefully orchestrated movements by large holders.

According to this parsing tool’s specific data set, which monitors more than 60,000 sleeping legacy wallets, the first quarter recorded 8,837.55 BTC across 217 transfers, followed by 9,824.29 BTC during the second quarter. Activity intensified between July and September, when 312 transfers moved 13,111.20 BTC, establishing the third quarter as the busiest period examined by our newsdesk.

As we reported previously, August was the standout month, producing 188 transfers totaling 6,427.59 BTC, equivalent to approximately 214 BTC daily. September followed with another 5,419.45 BTC, while May ranked third with 5,073.71 BTC.

July, conversely, registered just 1,264.16 BTC across 30 transfers, making it the quietest month. October subsequently recorded 2,159.15 BTC across 35 movements, although its average transaction size reached 61.69 BTC, the highest monthly average of the year.

The figures illustrate an interesting distinction: more wallet movements do not necessarily translate into greater bitcoin volume. Some periods featured numerous modest transfers, while others were dominated by a handful of exceptionally large holders moving substantial balances.

Satoshi-Era Bitcoin Awakens After More Than 16 Years

Perhaps the most fascinating developments involved bitcoin originating from 2010, when mining rewards were 50 BTC per block and the network remained in its infancy. On Saturday, Jan. 10, a wave of 40 addresses created between July and December 2010 collectively moved 2,000 BTC.

Each address contained approximately 50 BTC, and the transactions appeared within block 931668, occurring roughly three seconds apart over a two-minute interval. The coordinated movement accounted for nearly all the 2,020 BTC transferred that day, making Jan. 10 the largest single day for dormant bitcoin movements parsed by the blockchain tool in 2026.

Another extraordinary episode unfolded Saturday, Sept. 5, when addresses originating in March 2010 transferred their original 50 BTC balances within an 11-minute window. September ultimately recorded 600 BTC moving from 2010 wallets. Across the year so far til the end of October, legacy bitcoin addresses first created in 2010 transferred approximately 2,840 BTC, while wallets created in 2011 contributed at least another 815.99 BTC.

These movements are particularly interesting because their precise balances resemble original mining subsidies. However, the appearance of early block rewards does not establish that Satoshi Nakamoto controlled the addresses, nor does it identify their owners.

Moreover, none of the 2010 bitcoin movements documented in Bitcoin.com News reports have been linked to the Patoshi Pattern, the distinctive mining signature associated with pseudonymous Bitcoin creator Satoshi Nakamoto’s early mining activity.

Btcparser’s data also revealed unusual activity involving extremely small balances. Two 2010 wallets transferred just 0.00001093 BTC each on Sept. 9, illustrating how dormant-wallet monitoring can capture both substantial movements and tiny transactions associated with previously inactive addresses.

The Mystery of Bitcoin’s Repeated 500 BTC Transfers

Beyond ancient mining rewards, one of the year’s most intriguing patterns involved wallets established on Jan. 23, 2016.

Four addresses created on Jan. 23, 2016, each transferred exactly 500 BTC, with movements recorded on March 24, May 19, July 2, and Oct. 20, 2026. Together, those four transfers represented 2,000 BTC, approximately 5.9% of all dormant bitcoin tracked during the examined period.

The spacing between transactions suggests a potentially deliberate distribution schedule. Nevertheless, common creation dates and identical balances cannot independently establish that the addresses belong to the same individual or institution.

Other patterns were equally conspicuous. Nine wallets created Jan. 4, 2014, collectively transferred 837.25 BTC across February, May, and June. Another five wallets established the following day moved exactly 100 BTC apiece on March 31. Combined, those two groups accounted for 1,337.25 BTC.

Meanwhile, 61 addresses associated with a recurring 10 BTC transfer pattern moved 610 BTC during May and June. Another 56 wallets created in late 2016 transferred 599.71 BTC over May 2 and 3, including 40 transactions recorded within a single block.

Such concentrated activity suggests unique types of wallet management, consolidation, or coordinated custody operations rather than hundreds of unrelated holders independently deciding to transact simultaneously.

The year’s largest individual transfer came in early September, when a wallet established in 2016 moved approximately 1,260.78 BTC. That transaction was more than twice the size of the next-largest individual movement recorded.

Which Bitcoin Wallet Generations Moved the Most Coins?

Although Satoshi-era activity attracted considerable attention, wallets established several years later accounted for substantially more transferred bitcoin. Addresses originating in 2014 led the examined period with at least 8,134.20 BTC, followed closely by 2016 wallets with 7,941.98 BTC.

The 2013 cohort contributed 5,560.90 BTC, while addresses established in 2017 moved at least 4,163.11 BTC. Together, the 2014 and 2016 generations accounted for approximately 47% of the bitcoin tracked in the report. August was especially consequential for 2014 addresses. That cohort transferred 3,286.26 BTC across 94 movements, accounting for more than half the month’s bitcoin volume.

The 2016 generation displayed greater consistency, recording more than 500 BTC in every month from July through October. Its movements included the recurring 500 BTC transactions and September’s enormous 1,260.78 BTC transfer.

Another curious finding concerned transaction timing. During the first six months, Saturdays and Sundays accounted for 193 of 526 transfers, or 36.7%, despite representing approximately 29% of calendar days. Those weekend movements carried 8,269.77 BTC, equivalent to 44.3% of first-half volume. Saturday recorded the greatest bitcoin volume, while Sunday led in the number of transfers.

The concentration could reflect scheduled operational activity or favorable transaction conditions, although the available records cannot establish precisely why certain holders favored weekends.

What Exactly Does Btcparser Monitor?

Understanding Btcparser’s methodology is important when interpreting the figures. Its version 1 monitoring service was designed specifically to detect activity involving historically inactive bitcoin addresses, rather than measure every movement of previously dormant bitcoin across the network.

According to the service’s published description, Btcparser version 1 continuously monitors 64,529 addresses, including 21,519 originating in 2009, 12,396 from 2010, and 3,598 from 2011. Its historical address coverage extends through July 2017, with additional monitoring categories associated with the infamous Mt Gox theft and the Bitfinex hack.

However, the monitored population is selective. It does not represent every historical Bitcoin address, every address format, or every coin that has remained inactive for an extended period. The 33,932.19 BTC identified in the report, therefore, represents activity captured through the examined Btcparser records, not a comprehensive accounting of all dormant bitcoin revived in 2026.

Checkonchain Reveals More Than 227,000 BTC Revived in 2026

The broader picture becomes considerably more interesting when the Btcparser findings are compared with Checkonchain’s Total Revived Supply by Year Acquired (BTC) metric. According to the analytics provider’s stats, approximately 227,196.10 BTC acquired before 2019 (now worth $183.58 billion) had been revived during 2026, a figure substantially larger than the movements documented through the narrower Btcparser examination.

Of that amount, 186,123.72 BTC, or 81.9%, originated from coins acquired between 2015 and 2018. Another 27,653.01 BTC came from the 2012-2014 period, while just 13,419.37 BTC originated before 2012. These figures establish that the overwhelming majority of revived pre-2019 bitcoin originated from comparatively younger holdings, rather than the earliest years of Bitcoin’s existence.

Revived Pre-2019 Bitcoin Supply in 2026
Acquisition periodRevived BTCShare
Before 201213,419.375.9%
2012-201427,653.0112.2%
2015-2018186,123.7281.9%
Total227,196.10100%

Source: Checkonchain, as cited in Bitcoin.com News.

The distinction between the two datasets is essential. Btcparser documents specific movements from selected historically inactive addresses, while Checkonchain measures a broader category of revived supply based on acquisition periods. Consequently, the 33,932.19 BTC identified through Btcparser is equivalent to approximately 14.9% of Checkonchain’s larger pre-2019 revival figure.

That comparison illustrates the relative scale of the two measurements, rather than establishing a directly interchangeable subset. Ultimately, the two datasets tell complementary stories about the network’s aging supply. Btcparser exposes the individual movements, including ancient mining rewards, coordinated sweeps, and recurring multimillion-dollar transfers, while Checkonchain reveals the much larger volume of older coins returning to activity.

Neither measurement establishes that the bitcoin was sold. The evidence instead shows that long-held supply continues to move, even as the oldest coins represent only a modest fraction of the broader revival. The blockchain reveals when sleeping bitcoin awakens, but not necessarily why its owners have chosen to disturb it.

title: Standard Chartered Expands Prime Brokerage Partnership With 24X to Cover BTC and ETH
summary: 24X says Standard Chartered is expanding its prime-brokerage relationship to cover BTC and ETH. The arrangement is aimed at institutional…
content:
Institutional investors will be able to access Bitcoin and Ether trading through an expanded relationship between 24X and Standard Chartered. In a November 10 announcement, 24X Bermuda said the banking group will extend its prime-brokerage role from foreign-exchange products to digital assets on 24X’s multi-asset technology platform.

TL;DR: 24X says Standard Chartered is expanding its prime-brokerage relationship to cover BTC and ETH. The arrangement is aimed at institutional counterparties accessing crypto and FX through one execution infrastructure. It changes the trading and counterparty workflow for eligible participants; it is not a retail exchange rollout.

One relationship across different trading markets

The company’s stated model allows an institutional participant to face Standard Chartered as its central counterparty while using 24X for execution, matching, liquidity configuration and straight-through processing. That separation matters. The participant’s commercial relationship and credit exposure are handled differently from the technology that matches orders.

Traditional foreign exchange and spot cryptocurrency trading do not have identical market structures or risk profiles. FX markets have established bank relationships, while crypto markets operate around the clock and rely on a patchwork of exchanges, brokers and custody providers. An integrated platform can simplify some operational tasks, although it still requires clients to understand the product-specific terms.

The release says 24X already offered FX, non-deliverable forwards and spot services. BTC and ETH are the additional digital-asset instruments named in the expanded partnership. It would be misleading to claim the agreement immediately covers every token, derivative or jurisdiction.

Counterparty quality is not the same as risk elimination

A recognized bank acting as a central relationship may appeal to institutions that want more familiar onboarding, credit arrangements and oversight. It does not remove Bitcoin volatility, market liquidity problems or the possibility of disruptions in the surrounding infrastructure. Nor should the word ‘prime’ be used as a shortcut for saying all trades are insured or guaranteed.

Institutions will need to evaluate exposure limits, settlement timing, custody arrangements, collateral terms and what happens during market stress. The distinction between an execution venue and the organization responsible for a trading obligation is especially important for crypto, where the history of market failures has made counterparty concentration a persistent concern.

NewsBTC previously looked at Ripple Prime’s effort to bring traditional markets into 24-hour trading workflows. That is a distinct product and operator, but it reflects the same strategic demand: customers increasingly want to manage digital and conventional exposures without jumping between disconnected systems.

What should be confirmed next?

The announcement establishes the partnership expansion, but it does not provide a full ledger of live client trades, volumes or fee terms. Commercial success depends on whether eligible counterparties find the combined trading and brokerage model attractive enough to move business from existing venues.

As tokenized securities and digital assets enter more established markets, investors may become less focused on whether a blockchain is present and more concerned with the legal machinery behind settlement. Our report on the NYSE’s tokenized securities infrastructure partners describes why those arrangements matter. For 24X, the next proof point will be active institutional adoption rather than the breadth of the announcement alone.

Written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.

title: CFTC warns Kalshi of imminent charges over notification of contracts: Politico
summary: The prediction markets operator says the issue involves procedural errors affecting a handful of contracts, many of which weren’t live, according to Politico.
content:
Latest NewsPublishedNov 10, 2026

The prediction markets operator says the issue involves procedural errors affecting a handful of contracts, many of which weren’t live, according to Politico.

Prediction markets operator Kalshi is being warned of imminent charges from the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission over whether the operator properly notified the agency about new products, Politico reported Tuesday. 

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is investigating notifications involving dozens of products, the report said, citing a person with direct knowledge of the probe. The agency’s private notification to Kalshi suggests that charges could follow. 

The investigation has been underway for months, the person said. 

Speaking to Politico, Kalshi spokesperson Elisabeth Diana described the matter as a procedural error involving submissions for a handful of contracts, many of which never went live.

“We are already addressing the issue,” she added. 

The potential enforcement action comes as the CFTC fights to establish its exclusive authority over prediction markets, including by challenging state efforts to regulate Kalshi. 

Separately, Kalshi is backing the regulator in a separate legal battle over its authority. On Monday, the company joined Coinbase and four other firms in seeking permission to file a brief supporting the CFTC’s treatment of perpetual futures tied to individual US stocks.

Bitcoin Heated Hot Tubs and 278 Washington Bitcoin Merchants : Now Accepting Bitcoin
Washington Bitcoin merchants, from Seattle coffee shops to a Snorkel hot tub heated by bitcoin miners.
This post Bitcoin Heated Hot Tubs and 278 Washington Bitcoin Merchants : Now Accepting Bitcoin...
content:
Washington Bitcoin merchant list has 278 businesses, from coffee shops and salons to a hot tub maker that heats its tubs with bitcoin mining. The list spans 94 named cities, and Seattle leads the way with 46 listings. First up is a homegrown US manufacturing business from Washington that makes a super unique product.

Snorkel: A Hot Tub Maker That Heats With Bitcoin

Snorkel has been making hot tubs in the Pacific Northwest since 1979, and its wood-stove business dates to the late 1970s. What makes them special is their full cedar tubs, and the wood stove which is fully submerged into the water of the cedar hot tub and has the “snorkel” coming out of the water. This is very convenient for anyone who has no electrical hook up.

It started with a bet in 2025. Michael Diederich, the owner, began accepting bitcoin for hot tubs after a wager with his brother. Payments were slow to trickle in at first, but bitcoiners kept asking him to build a hot tub powered by bitcoin miners. He started building one, pairing the tub with miners that heat the water. Snorkel works with Dane Soja of Hashrate House on the build.

The prototype with two S19J Pro miners drawing about 8 kW, which it says heated a tub from cold to 104°F (40°C) in under four hours. The project won an innovation award at the Heat Punk Summit in Denver, and a Snorkel tub is on display in Denver. Diederich sees a future where every electric hot tub is heated by miners, because the mining income helps pay back the cost of energy that would otherwise be wasted as heat.

The Rose Gift House and Coffee, Renton

The Rose sits at 226 Main Ave S in downtown Renton, in the Old Renton Pub building. Owner Katie Newman opened it in October 2020 as a gift shop that happened to serve coffee, and the coffee side grew into the larger part of the business. The shop stocks locally roasted coffee, handpicked artisan goods, and grab-and-go food. It won Best Customer Service in the 2025 Best of Renton readers’ poll.

Overcast Coffee, Seattle

Overcast Coffee is on Capitol Hill, and it started as a walk-up counter at 312 15th Ave E beside Kaiser Permanente. Owner Jonathan Pak opened the first shop there in June 2020. A second location, at 1517 12th Ave inside the Metier bike complex, came later, and the company buys its coffee and ingredients from small, local Seattle businesses.

title: Global banks commit $270M to stablecoin venture targeting 2027 launch
summary: Project Faro, backed by Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and BBVA, has secured $270 million in funding to launch a US dollar stablecoin in the first half of 2027.
content:
A consortium of 21 financial institutions has committed about $270 million in funding to a stablecoin initiative known as Project Faro. The project, backed by big banks, aims to act as a stablecoin issuer and launch a US dollar stablecoin in the first half of 2027.

According to Bloomberg, the funding is intended to cover five years of operations for the new company, which plans to issue stablecoins pegged to the currencies of all G7 countries, with a euro-backed coin expected to follow the dollar launch.

The group first announced the initiative in September. While confirmed details are thin, people familiar with the matter said the company is expected to be incorporated in the US, Bloomberg reported. 

The group includes banks such as Citigroup, Goldman Sachs, Banco Santander, Deutsche Bank and BBVA. Similar initiatives are also underway, including Stripe-led Open USD, which counts Visa among its founding partners, and Qivalis, a European banking consortium seeking to challenge the dominance of US dollar-pegged stablecoins.

Overlap with rival consortiums

BBVA is one of several Faro members also involved in competing stablecoin initiatives, including Open USD and Qivalis. Dutch lender Rabobank is also a Faro member and joined Qivalis in May, when the euro consortium added 25 banks to reach 37 members. BNP Paribas was among the 10 banks that first explored what became Faro in October 2025 and later joined Qivalis. 

Qivalis has since made progress on the regulatory front, receiving authorization from the Dutch central bank as an electronic money institution in October 2026. The consortium is preparing to launch a fully regulated, euro-denominated stablecoin, with plans to make it available for payments, cross-border settlements and tokenized asset transactions.

The overlap highlights how traditional financial institutions are positioning themselves across multiple initiatives rather than committing exclusively to a single stablecoin issuance project.

By participating in competing projects, banks can explore different approaches to issuing and distributing digital currencies while retaining a stake in the infrastructure that could underpin future payment and settlement systems.

Related: BofA, Citi, Goldman Sachs among 21 institutions planning stablecoin launch

A crowded room

Despite the growing institutional interest, Faro is entering a market dominated by two crypto-native issuers.

Tether’s USDT and Circle’s USDC account for approximately 85% of the roughly $290 billion stablecoin market as of Nov. 10, according to DefiLlama. USDT had a market capitalization of approximately $176.3 billion, while USDC accounted for around $70.4 billion.

Distribution could, however, offer the bank-backed venture a competitive advantage. Faro’s participating institutions already have established banking customers, payment networks and relationships with businesses and financial institutions that could help distribute a new stablecoin.

Rather than building an entirely new customer base, the consortium could leverage those existing relationships to introduce its stablecoin to new audiences, including retail users. Open USD, developed by the Open Standard consortium, is pursuing a similar approach by bringing together payment providers, banks, financial technology companies and merchants around a shared stablecoin infrastructure.

The challenge for both will be translating their existing financial infrastructure and customer relationships into a competitive onchain payment network.

title: Visa Adds Monad to Stablecoin Settlement Options as Institutions Seek More Rails
summary: Monad has been added to Visa's stablecoin settlement options for participating institutional clients, according to a statement from the Monad…
content:
Visa’s growing list of blockchain settlement options reportedly has a new entrant: Monad. According to a November 10 report citing the Monad Foundation, participating Visa issuers and acquirers can now use the network for stablecoin settlement. That is a back-office financial infrastructure development, rather than a new consumer-facing Visa card that automatically makes every merchant accept cryptocurrency.

TL;DR: Monad has been added to Visa’s stablecoin settlement options for participating institutional clients, according to a statement from the Monad Foundation reported on November 10. A privacy capability is planned, not yet delivered. The important test will be actual institutional usage and the operational conditions attached to settlement.

What is changing for banks and payment providers?

When a cardholder pays at a shop, the retail transaction and the subsequent movement of funds between financial institutions are separate processes. A settlement service can use digital dollars on a blockchain to transfer value between participating institutions without requiring consumers to interact with a crypto wallet. That is the layer Visa has been expanding.

Visa’s October 15 update on stablecoin-powered money movement showed that parts of its broader digital-dollar strategy were moving from pilots toward live commercial deployment. Monad’s reported addition extends the selection of networks available to eligible partners; it should not be confused with a universal launch in every market or for every Visa transaction.

For an issuer or acquirer, more than one usable settlement rail can provide choices around transaction processing, cost, operational resilience and supported assets. But multiple chains also bring added technical and compliance responsibilities. Connecting a network is the beginning of integration, not proof that it will process meaningful volumes immediately.

Monad is competing on performance, but privacy matters too

Monad is designed for high-throughput smart-contract execution. The latest announcement also points to a proposed privacy feature intended to shield institutional settlement details from general public view while allowing access for authorized reviewers, including auditors and regulators. That capability is described as coming in future months, so it should not be reported as an existing production guarantee.

The distinction is important. Institutions often need to protect commercially sensitive flows, yet they must also meet audit, recordkeeping and sanctions obligations. Privacy without permitted oversight would not meet all of those needs. Future deployment documentation should explain how access controls work and who can inspect what information.

NewsBTC previously examined how Visa’s treasury engine targets institutional settlement. Separately, Reap’s Monad-linked card infrastructure plan illustrates a different use of the same chain: backing consumer card activity, not necessarily settling balances between institutions.

Adoption must be measured in completed settlement

A blockchain being listed among supported options can improve its credibility with enterprise developers, but that does not establish a direct relationship between network adoption and the market price of its native token. Fees, throughput, partner concentration and the way transaction costs are paid all influence the economics.

What matters next is confirmation of which issuers and acquirers are live, which stablecoins and regions are supported, how settlement is reconciled when something fails, and what measurable transaction volume arrives. Those details would turn a promising infrastructure announcement into evidence of commercial activity. Until then, this is a meaningful new option—not an automatic overhaul of how Visa payments work everywhere.

Written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.

title: Near AI Confirms Security Breach Affecting 100 Users and 18 Agents
summary: Near AI disclosed a security breach that exposed account information belonging to approximately 100 users and compromised data from 18 legacy artificial intelligence (AI) agents. The Nov. 8, 2026, intrusion exploited a vulnerability in an open-source inference engine, potentially exposing confidenti...
content:
Near AI disclosed a security breach that exposed account information belonging to approximately 100 users and compromised data from 18 legacy artificial intelligence (AI) agents. The Nov. 8, 2026, intrusion exploited a vulnerability in an open-source inference engine, potentially exposing confidential AI requests.

Key Takeaways

  • An SGLang vulnerability allowed an attacker to execute code on a Near AI inference server and penetrate internal infrastructure.
  • Approximately 100 user accounts and 18 legacy AI agents were affected, while two customers had API keys exposed.
  • Near AI restored Cloud services after patching its servers, but acknowledged limitations in confidential computing protections.

SGLang Vulnerability Opens Door to Near AI Infrastructure

According to Near AI’s official security incident report published Monday, Nov. 9, the unauthorized party exploited a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in SGLang, an open-source engine used to process artificial intelligence workloads. The flaw permitted code execution on one inference server, providing an entry point into additional internal systems.

From there, the intruder reached infrastructure associated with Near AI’s previously deprecated Private Chat service, downloading account information belonging to approximately 100 users. The stolen records included names and email addresses, while certain accounts also exposed subscription plans and balance information.

The intrusion extended beyond customer records. Investigators confirmed unauthorized access to 18 agents operating on a legacy Near AI Agents deployment outside the company’s trusted execution environment (TEE). Retrieved information included chat histories, configuration settings, and operational logs.

Two Near AI Cloud customers also had application programming interface (API) keys exposed through those logs. Both credentials have since been revoked.

Importantly, Near AI reported finding no indication that stored Private Chat conversations or uploaded files were accessed. However, the company acknowledged that requests processed on the compromised server on Nov. 8 could have been observed, including requests operating in confidential mode.

The disclosure distinguishes confirmed data theft from potential exposure of information during processing. Near AI did not quantify how many confidential requests might have been observed.

Why Didn’t Confidential Computing Prevent the Breach?

Perhaps the incident’s most consequential revelation concerns the limitations of confidential computing, a technology designed to protect sensitive information through hardware-isolated execution environments. Near AI explained that these protections cannot automatically defend against vulnerabilities within the applications operating inside those environments.

“Confidential computing protects data from the operator and the host. It does not protect against a vulnerability in the software running inside the environment, and that is what happened here,” the company acknowledged.

In practical terms, the attacker exploited the inference software itself, rather than needing to defeat the hardware isolation mechanisms. Once the malicious code executed inside the affected server, requests undergoing processing became potentially accessible.

The distinction matters because confidential computing is intended to restrict access by infrastructure operators and underlying hosts. It does not guarantee that the software handling sensitive information is free from exploitable defects. Near AI said its security analysis would now examine inference software and surrounding services with the same rigor applied to protected computing environments.

Near AI Restores Cloud Services Following Security Response

Following detection, Near AI revoked active sessions and administrative credentials, replaced agent tokens, and took Private Chat offline. Engineers deployed a fix for the SGLang vulnerability across every inference server and completed additional credential rotations.

The company also reported completing a forensic review, notifying affected users and contacting the owners of all 18 compromised AI agents individually. Near AI confirmed that cloud service access had been restored after containment and remediation. The vulnerability was additionally reported to the SGLang project.

Affected customers received instructions through security@near.ai, while the company cautioned users against unsolicited communications referencing account information or balances. Regulatory notifications will follow where legally required. The incident reportedly did not affect Near Protocol itself or other services within the broader ecosystem.

Nevertheless, the breach raises an uncomfortable question for confidential AI infrastructure providers: How private is protected computation when the software processing requests remains vulnerable? Hardware isolation offers an important security boundary, but the Near AI incident demonstrates that confidentiality ultimately depends on the integrity of the applications operating within it.

The Near AI compromise also arrives amid an extraordinary succession of security incidents documented by Bitcoin.com News over the past few months. From Binance’s staggering $6.3 billion hack on Oct. 29 and Bitget’s reported $387.5 million wallet breach to the Liquid Network exploit involving nearly 600 BTC, attackers have repeatedly exposed weaknesses across the digital asset industry.

Security incidents involving Ledger, Safepal, Trezor, Keystone, Chainalysis, Gnosis Pay, Keplr-Web3Auth, and Crédit Mutuel Arkéa have further broadened the concerns, while newly disclosed iOS vulnerabilities threaten sensitive application data. Collectively, these episodes reveal an increasingly uncomfortable reality: The industry’s security challenges extend far beyond stolen cryptocurrency, reaching deep into customer records, software dependencies, authentication systems, and the infrastructure entrusted with protecting digital assets.

title: Tessera – SpaceX Exposure From a One-Dollar Solana Wallet
summary: Chan Ahn is Founder and CEO of Tessera, a Solana-based platform that issues tokens tracking the economic performance of late-stage private companies such as SpaceX, OpenAI, xAI and Kalshi, tradable permissionlessly on decentralized exchanges. Before crypto, Chan spent more than 15 years in tradition...
content:
Skip to content

Chan Ahn is Founder and CEO of Tessera, a Solana-based platform that issues tokens tracking the economic performance of late-stage private companies such as SpaceX, OpenAI, xAI and Kalshi, tradable permissionlessly on decentralized exchanges. Before crypto, Chan spent more than 15 years in traditional finance at Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan and Credit Suisse, specializing in derivatives, structured products and private markets, and he holds a PhD in computational finance from Imperial College.

The link will open a new window. Click the menu and down arrow to download the file.

Why you should listen

Chan’s starting point is a structural shift most retail investors have not noticed. Companies are staying private far longer, and by the time they list, the valuation has grown so large that the IPO works more as a payday for insiders than an opportunity for everyone else. Pension funds and other institutions routinely hold 20 to 30 percent of their portfolios in private assets, while most individual investors hold none. Chan explains why: buying a secondary stake in a company like Kalshi typically means finding a specialist broker, clearing KYC, paying lawyers to draft bespoke documents, negotiating for weeks with no visible price, then spending another month verifying where the shares came from. From first call to closing can take three to four months, and accreditation rules keep most people from attempting it at all.

Tessera’s answer is a deliberate choice of structure, and Chan is unusually candid about it. Rather than tokenizing shares directly, Tessera holds the underlying stock in bankruptcy-remote entities in the Cayman Islands and issues tokens representing loan participation rights. Holders get the economic exposure but no ownership, voting or dividend rights. Chan argues this is closer to how most retail investors already hold fractional shares through a broker than they realize, and says it has allowed Tessera to obtain a legal opinion that the tokens are not securities under Singapore law. The practical result is that anyone with a Solana wallet and as little as a dollar can trade on Meteora or Jupiter without KYC, with the US, China and sanctioned jurisdictions excluded. The model has already been tested in production: SpaceX’s June IPO triggered a redemption cycle, and Chan describes how the holding entity is selling down the stock, with roughly a fifth sold so far, and returning USDC to token holders pro rata.

The conversation then turns to the AI listing wave, where Chan has been a notably disciplined voice. Disclosing that Tessera offers OpenAI exposure but nothing linked to Anthropic, he explains the simple discounted cash flow model he built to test Anthropic’s IPO valuation. By his estimate, it requires revenue and margins to keep expanding at about 20 percent a year for a decade. He is firmly bullish on AI as a transformative technology but cautions that being right about a technology is not the same as being right about each security or the timing. In the hot take round, Chan describes himself as a Bitcoin maximalist of a particular kind: after building on Bitcoin himself, he lost faith in a Bitcoin application economy but came to see those limits as strengthening its case as a store of value in a multipolar world. He names blockchain becoming part of everyday life as his firmest conviction, with tokenization as one step toward it, and picks The Three-Body Problem as his favorite science fiction.

title: Here’s what happened in crypto today
summary: Need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation.
content:
Today in crypto, hotter-than-expected US inflation raised concerns about a larger Federal Reserve interest rate hike in December, Coinbase and Kalshi joined four other firms backing the CFTC in a lawsuit over single-stock perpetual futures, and cybersecurity firm CertiK urged crypto exchanges to impose hard dollar limits on hot-wallet holdings.

Hot US inflation raises odds of half-point Fed hike in December

Crypto industry experts warned on Tuesday that higher-than-expected US inflation could lead to a another Federal Reserve interest rate hike, making borrowing more expensive and potentially discouraging investment in cryptocurrencies.

The US Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.4% month over month in October, above economists’ forecast of 0.3%, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics - a slower increase than September’s 0.6% rise. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, rose 0.3%, above the expected 0.2%.

Currently, the Federal Reserve holds its benchmark interest rate at 3.75% to 4.00%, after raising it by a quarter-point in September and leaving it unchanged in October.

The report came just a few hours after Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said in London that another core inflation reading of 0.3% or higher could prompt the Fed to consider a larger interest rate hike in December.

“In that case, I believe a 50-basis-point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting,” Waller said. “Hiking only 25-basis-points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take.”

Coinbase, Kalshi join lawsuit backing CFTC over US stock perp futures

Coinbase, Kalshi and four other companies asked a federal court Monday to accept a brief backing the United States Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) in a lawsuit over perpetual futures tied to individual US stocks.

According to a proposed amicus brief shared Monday by Coinbase legal representative Molly Abraham, the group also includes Kraken parent Payward, trading companies DRW Holdings and Jump Trading, and crypto investment company Paradigm Operations. The companies argue that stock perpetual futures fall under existing US futures laws.

The filing comes days after a federal judge found that the CFTC likely “exceeded its statutory authority” in allowing single-stock perpetuals to trade as security futures.

The case could determine whether US exchanges can offer retail traders contracts that track individual stocks without expiring.

On Nov. 3, the CFTC announced that single-stock perpetual futures, or stock perps, could begin trading on US-regulated exchanges for the first time.

The Capital Markets Alliance Association (CMAA), a newly formed trade and advocacy group representing traditional financial market participants and whose members include Cboe and Citadel Securities, sued the CFTC last week, challenging the CFTC’s authority to allow the contracts to trade.

Crypto exchanges need dollar caps on hot wallets, CertiK says

Crypto exchanges should impose hard dollar limits on their hot-wallet holdings rather than relying solely on cold-storage ratios to measure security, according to cybersecurity firm CertiK.

The recommendation came as several crypto exchanges recently disclosed how much they held in cold wallets, seeking to reassure customers after the record Binance hack that targeted its hot wallets. Crypto exchange Gate reported that 88.26% of its total assets were in cold storage, while Coinbase said it keeps more than 99% of customer assets offline. 

“Cold storage is a useful measure of online exposure, but it is not a standalone security score,” CertiK’s research team told Cointelegraph. 

CertiK said crypto exchanges should consider setting hot-wallet caps for each asset and blockchain according to the strictest of three limits: a percentage of customer liabilities, estimated withdrawal needs and an absolute loss ceiling based on the exchange’s financial resources and recovery capabilities. 

“Flexibility should support operating liquidity, while hard dollar ceilings and circuit breakers limit potential loss,” they said.

title: Strategy Adds 1,036 BTC While Repurchasing $188M of STRC Preferred Shares
summary: Strategy has disclosed a 1,036-BTC purchase alongside $188 million of STRC repurchases. The combination shows that the company's Bitcoin strategy…
content:
Strategy’s newest capital-allocation update contains two transactions that point in different directions. In a November 9 filing announcement, the company said it acquired 1,036 additional Bitcoin and bought back approximately $188 million of STRC preferred shares. The first adds to exposure to BTC; the second reduces outstanding securities in its wider financing structure.

TL;DR: Strategy has disclosed a 1,036-BTC purchase alongside $188 million of STRC repurchases. The combination shows that the company’s Bitcoin strategy involves ongoing capital management, not simply accumulation. These are separate transactions with different effects on liquidity, risk and future obligations.

A purchase is only one side of the strategy

Strategy is closely associated with long-term Bitcoin accumulation, and for good reason: its treasury is far larger than that of most public companies. Yet the recurring filings increasingly include details about preferred securities, reserves and capital raising that are central to understanding how that position is financed.

A Bitcoin purchase turns available funds into an asset whose market value can change around the clock. Repurchasing preferred shares does something else. It reduces the quantity of a security issued to outside investors and may alter future distribution obligations, depending on that security’s terms. One action raises direct BTC exposure; the other changes the claims that investors have on Strategy’s capital structure.

That distinction was visible in an earlier update covered by NewsBTC, when Strategy bought 811 BTC and repurchased $208.2 million of STRC. The new announcement continues that paired approach, rather than revealing a sudden switch away from its central investment thesis.

Why the preferred-share repurchase deserves attention

Preferred securities can offer investors contractual distributions or other rights that differ from ordinary equity. Their terms, market prices and the company’s reserve position matter for both existing holders and common shareholders. Buying them back may be attractive when they trade at prices the issuer considers advantageous, but it also uses liquidity that could otherwise remain in reserve or fund more purchases.

There is a useful comparison with other Bitcoin treasury companies, which have their own funding methods and varying tolerance for leverage. The phrase ‘corporate Bitcoin buyer’ hides important differences in debt maturities, preferred distributions, equity issuance and the sources of cash used to acquire coins.

The right way to interpret the new holding total

Strategy’s public metrics indicate Bitcoin holdings around 850,364 BTC following the update. Readers should use the company’s dated disclosure when comparing holdings and purchase prices rather than combining a fresh transaction with an older snapshot. Market-value figures can change between the filing and the moment a reader opens the article.

Another consideration is the difference between a repurchase authorization and completed repurchases. Here the company is describing actual STRC repurchase activity, which should be counted separately from any standing authority to buy securities later. The price paid and reduction in outstanding shares determine its economic impact; simply repeating the dollar amount cannot answer those questions.

None of this proves that the company’s securities or Bitcoin will rise. A more useful test is whether Strategy can keep servicing its obligations while making purchases in a period of changing interest rates and volatile digital-asset prices. The November 9 announcement confirms it is still doing both jobs—adding coins and adjusting the financing architecture that supports the strategy.

Written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.
